artifacts.summary: Re-derives the four repo-scoped lock call sites, finds three (not one) gate-acquire wiring points, confirms the named-mutex family is mkdir-based with no flock and no PID-liveness reclaim, measures the XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/run/user/UID/tmp fallback chain on the live host, and recommends parameterizing acquire_named_mutex with a base-directory argument plus a new opt-in gate-acquire-host/gate-release-host subcommand pair and a cross-directory double-start test.

memory_candidates.content: task-lock.sh's acquire_named_mutex family (.scope-lock/.commit-lock/.gate-lock) uses mkdir-based atomicity and purely time-elapsed staleness reclaim -- no flock, no PID-liveness check anywhere. A PID-liveness fast path was prototyped and reverted (see task-lock.sh:674-694 comment): the recorded pid for a {scope,commit,gate}-acquire CLI invocation is always the short-lived acquiring subprocess's own $$, not the long-lived holder (e.g. verify-deploy.sh), so a dead-pid check against it misclassifies a live holder as dead. This is a separate mechanism from the per-task .lock/holder.json family (cmd_acquire/cmd_reap), which DOES have PID-liveness via session_liveness()/kill -0 -- the two are easy to conflate but share no code path.

The gate layer's single-flight bracket (task-lock.sh's gate-acquire/gate-release) has THREE independent call sites, not one: tests/run-all.sh's top level, and TWO inside verify-deploy.sh (gate8_run() and a second gate-8-sibling battery). Any change to how/when the gate mutex is acquired must account for all three identically-shaped guard blocks (skip if narrowed/--only, skip if nested, run as guest if GATE_MUTEX_HELD inherited, else acquire-and-export) or risk leaving one entry point on the old behavior.

On this host (systemd/elogind), XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/$UID is tmpfs, mode 0700, owned by that uid, and per pam_systemd(8) is created at first login and removed at final logout (so never survives reboot either). An abandoned lock/file placed there is reclaimed by the OS independent of any application-level staleness window, but the same man page explicitly warns applications must still tolerate stale files across a logout/login cycle (same path can be reused by an unrelated new session). /tmp on this host is ext3/ext4-backed (not tmpfs), mode 1777 (world-writable + sticky), cleaned periodically by systemd-tmpfiles' tmp.conf by file age on boot, not wiped wholesale at reboot -- making it the MOST durable of a three-tier XDG_RUNTIME_DIR -> /run/user/$UID -> /tmp fallback chain, not the least. hooks/tts-notify.sh already has a working two-tier precedent: COOLDOWN_FILE="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/claude-tts-cooldown-${UID:-0}-${WEZTERM_PANE:-nopane}" -- UID-qualifying the filename to stay safe on a shared, world-writable /tmp.
